mappings.note: Framing your own questions to Yama requires grasping what the Katha Upanishad's Nachiketa was after - an ancient system of thought (LO-150) known through a literary work (LO-136).
Sets out and comments on Buddhism's central ideas; exactly the analysis of an ancient system of thought that LO-150 names. Not LO-136, since no single text's contents are at issue.
Unpacks the Buddha's saying that bathing does not purify - an argument about inner conduct against ritual, so a value of an ancient system of thought.
The central tenets of Jainism, the counterpart of the Buddhism item and under the same outcome; the frame offers one outcome for doctrinal content.
Beteille on tribal and Hindu traditions enriching each other: a claim about human diversity in India (LO-141) worked through religious systems (LO-150).
Asks the pupil to list the deities and festivals of their OWN region - describing diversity around her or him (LO-141) in its religious form (LO-150).
Documents local tribal groups, their art and their beliefs; the clearest LO-141 item in the chapter, since the demand is to describe diversity in the pupil's own surroundings.

True/false set covering the age of the Vedas, ekam sat, whether Jainism branched from Buddhism and what tribal belief covers: doctrinal claims (LO-150) alongside facts about the texts themselves (LO-136).
Staging Yama and several Nachiketas demands the Upanishadic dialogue's substance (LO-150) as the text presents it (LO-136). Mapped like the written version of the same exercise.
The tree with many roots and branches stands for the whole chapter's argument about one culture with many growths - a synthesis across developments, so LO-140 rather than any single doctrine.
'Veda' from the root vid, knowledge - a fact about the text and its name. LO-136 is used here for facts ABOUT the ancient works; LO-150 is kept for the ideas inside them.
Oral recitation as the means of transmitting the hymns for generations; a fact about how the literary work survived, so LO-136. Not LO-134, which concerns sources used to reconstruct history.
Where the Rig Veda was composed: a fact about the text (LO-136) tied to the Sapta Sindhava river country (LO-132).

UNESCO's recognition of Vedic chanting as intangible heritage is India's contribution in culture, which LO-149 names. Not LO-136, since the item is about the world's recognition rather than the text's content.
Rishis and rishikas as the male and female seers who composed the hymns - the authorship of the literary works, hence LO-136.
That the Vedic seers held the many deities to be one underlying reality is a doctrinal claim, so LO-150 rather than a fact about the text.
Janas as the clans of early Vedic society; social organisation in the ancient period, which LO-138 covers. Not LO-141, whose diversity is that of the pupil's own society today.
Sabha and samiti as early assemblies - a development in ancient governance, so LO-138. Not LO-145, whose levels of government are those of the Indian Union today.
The Upanishads bringing in rebirth and karma: new ideas of an ancient system of thought (LO-150) carried by a named body of texts (LO-136).
Brahman as the one divine essence in Vedanta - a core philosophical concept, so LO-150.
Atman as the inner Self; the companion concept to brahman and, like it, a doctrine rather than a textual fact.
The prayer sarve bhavantu sukhinah read as the Upanishadic sense of interconnected life - a VALUE of an ancient system of thought, which LO-150 names explicitly.
Lumbini as the Buddha's birthplace. LO-135 is not cited because it asks for sites on an outline map of INDIA and Lumbini lies in Nepal; the item's substance is the founder of an ancient tradition.
The Four Sights of old age, sickness and death driving Siddhartha's renunciation - the origin of the Buddhist analysis of suffering, so LO-150.
Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya: a founding moment of the tradition (LO-150) at a site in Bihar that can be placed on the map of India (LO-135), unlike Lumbini.
'Buddha' as the awakened one - the meaning of the title and so of the attainment the tradition is built on.
Avidya and attachment as the roots of suffering; the doctrinal core of Buddhism, hence LO-150.
Ahimsa as non-harming in thought, word and deed - a shared value of these ancient traditions, which is LO-150's 'values' clause.
Vardhamana born near Vaishali in Bihar: the founder of Jainism (LO-150) at a place locatable on the map of India (LO-135), mapped like the Bodh Gaya item.
'Jina' as the conqueror of inner passions - the idea behind the name Jain, so a doctrinal item.
Aparigraha as non-possession; a Jain ethical principle, and again the values clause of LO-150.
The Jataka tales and what they are FOR: stories in a body of ancient literature (LO-136) carrying Buddhist virtues (LO-150).
Rohineya the burglar as a Jain narrative about right conduct and second chances - a story from the tradition's literature (LO-136) teaching its values (LO-150).

Ellora holding Hindu, Buddhist and Jain rock-cut work side by side: the point is the coexistence of three ancient traditions (LO-150) at one Indian site (LO-135). Not LO-148, whose subject is contact with regions OUTSIDE India.
The anthropological definition of a tribe - shared descent, culture, language and territory; the vocabulary of human diversity in LO-141.
About 705 Scheduled Tribes in the 2011 figures; a measure of India's human diversity, so LO-141 rather than a religion outcome.
Reverence for nature as common ground between Hindu, folk and tribal belief: a shared value across systems of thought (LO-150) held by diverse communities (LO-141).
Vedic Sanskrit as the language of the hymns; a fact about the literary works, mapped with the other text items rather than with the doctrines.
Buddhism and Jainism rejecting the authority of the Vedas - a comparison between ancient systems of thought, squarely LO-150.
Matches anekantavada to Jainism against Charvaka, Buddhist and Lokayata distractors; the item turns on which doctrine belongs to which school, so LO-150.
